wine.name: Bandol La Tourtine
wine.grapes: Mourvèdre, the great majority, with Grenache and Cinsault for the rest.
wine.sites: La Tourtine, a windswept slope by Le Castellet in sun from dawn to dusk; the domaine gives its soil as Santonian sandstone and marl with gypsum at the surface, and elsewhere as fairly deep and rich in clay. Cabassaou lies at its foot, out of the mistral.
wine.making: Sorted by hand, destemmed and crushed, the grapes are fermented with their own yeasts in concrete vats for three or four weeks; the wine is then aged for about eighteen months in large oak foudres before bottling, where the appellation asks a red for at least eighteen months in wood.
wine.glass: Black olive, blackberry and dark plum over wild thyme, liquorice and a meaty, leathery edge; dense and firm, with high, grippy tannin, fresh acidity and a long, savoury finish.
wine.ageing: Tannic and closed when young, it then opens into leather, game and dried herbs; the domaine gives it five to twenty years in a cool cellar.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle an hour or two ahead, an old one gently off its sediment; a large red wine glass.

label.means: The appellation of 1941 around the port west of Toulon, its red at least half Mourvèdre.
The parcel by Le Castellet whose grapes the domaine vinifies and bottles apart.

records.table: Windswept and sunny from dawn to dusk, La Tourtine is the slope by Le Castellet behind Domaine Tempier's Bandol red of that name: mostly Mourvèdre, aged about eighteen months in large oak foudres. Dark, savoury and firm, with black olive and wild thyme, it needs years and a decanter.
records.story: The farm at Le Plan du Castellet had been in the Tempier family since 1834 when, in 1936, Lucie Tempier, called Lulu (1917 to 2020), married a young man who had studied farming at Aix, and her father gave the couple the estate. They settled there in 1940. Her husband set out to show that Bandol could make reds to age beside the classic wines of France, built on Mourvèdre, a late ripening grape that the warmth of the sea suits; by the domaine's account he was the spiritual father of the appellation, granted by a decree of 11 November 1941. The domaine bottled its first wine, a rosé, in 1943, and its first red followed in 1951. In 1968 the family built a cellar of large foudres for long ageing, and the couple's two sons ran the domaine and its cellar for the decades that followed. Over the years the family found that its parcels gave different wines, and it came to vinify and bottle La Tourtine, La Migoua and Cabassaou apart. Lulu's cooking, and the long lunches at the domaine, became famous far beyond Bandol. Bandol rouge has its historical answer in Tempier, and La Tourtine gives that answer from a single parcel.

others.name: Bandol Cuvée Lulu & Lucien
others.note: The domaine's main red, a Mourvèdre led blend from across its vineyards, called Cuvée Classique until the family renamed it for the founding couple with the 2020 reds.

others.name: Bandol Cabassaou
others.note: From a small sheltered parcel below La Tourtine, out of the mistral: the red with the most Mourvèdre.

others.name: Bandol Rosé
others.note: Mourvèdre with Grenache and Cinsault, a rosé made to age; the domaine's first wine, in 1943, was a rosé.

traps: La Tourtine, La Migoua and Cabassaou are three parcels of one domaine, not three estates: Cabassaou carries the most Mourvèdre and La Migoua the least.
Bandol rouge is built on Mourvèdre, at least half the blend by law, with at least eighteen months in wood; it is not a Grenache led red.
Domaine Tempier lies at Le Plan du Castellet, inland of the port: Bandol names the appellation, not the village of the vines.

questions.q: The couple who took on Domaine Tempier in 1940 helped bring about the Bandol appellation. In what year was it granted by decree?
questions.exp: A decree of 11 November 1941 granted Bandol its appellation; 1936 was the year of the marriage that gave the couple the estate, and 1968 the year of the foudre cellar.

No source searched gave the first vintage bottled apart for La Tourtine; one search summary drawn from the estate's pages put the separate vinification of La Tourtine and La Migoua at 1960, another found nothing, so no year is given.
The domaine's own pages call its 1968 cellar the salle des foudres; that La Tourtine ages in that cellar was not confirmed and is not said.
The plan's merge note asked whether the rosé or the Classique is the wine the domaine is known by: no source searched said so, so no swap is proposed; both stand in others.

wine.name: Château Simone Palette Blanc
wine.grapes: Clairette, the great majority, with Grenache Blanc, Bourboulenc, Ugni Blanc and a little Muscat Blanc.
wine.sites: North facing slopes of the Montaiguet massif above the river Arc at Meyreuil, in a bowl sheltered from the wind, on limestone scree laid down in Tertiary lakes; some plots, replanted after phylloxera, are more than a century old.
wine.making: The grapes, picked by hand and sorted, go to a vertical press and ferment with native yeasts; by the estate's account the white is then raised for eighteen months in small oak foudres, six of them on its fine lees, and for a year in barrels before bottling, in the cellars that Carmelite friars dug in the sixteenth century.
wine.glass: Fennel, beeswax and lime blossom over almond, quince and a touch of honey; full in body and broad rather than sharp, with a waxy texture, gentle acidity and a long, nutty finish.
wine.ageing: Reserved at first, it gains honey, nut and wax with bottle age over many years.
wine.serve: 10 to 13 degrees Celsius, cool rather than cold, so the wax and nut show; no need to decant; a large white wine glass.

label.means: The small appellation just east of Aix, recognised on 28 April 1948, for red, white and rosé.
The estate at Meyreuil, in the Rougier family's hands since 1830.

records.table: Very old vines, mostly Clairette, on north facing slopes above the Arc near Aix give Château Simone's Palette Blanc, raised long in small oak foudres and then in barrels. Full, waxy and nutty, with fennel and honey, it is a white to pour cool with food.
records.story: The Carmelite friars of Aix, the Grands Carmes, held the old bastide on which Château Simone stands in the sixteenth century, and dug the cellars beneath it, which by the estate's account keep the steady temperature and natural humidity that suit ageing wine. The Rougier family has held the property since 1830, and later generations enlarged the cellars. After phylloxera the family replanted the vineyard on north facing slopes of the Montaiguet massif, in a sheltered bowl crossed by the river Arc, and some of those plots are more than a century old. In the 1940s, as the estate tells it, a member of the family won from the INAO recognition of an appellation for Château Simone itself, and by a decree of 28 April 1948 that recognition was extended into the appellation of Palette, a few hillsides at Meyreuil and its neighbours just east of Aix. The estate has kept a long roll of old varieties and the habit of long ageing in wood, in white, red and rosé alike. Say Palette at the table and Château Simone is the name to follow it; its white shows how far a Provençal white can go with age.

Château Simone's vines face north, on slopes above the Arc, against the picture of Provence as sun baked southern hillsides.

wine.name: Domaine de Trévallon Rouge
wine.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon and Syrah in about equal parts, the blend on which the estate made its name.
wine.sites: Plots cleared from limestone scrub across three small valleys on the north side of the Alpilles at Saint-Étienne-du-Grès, on very stony clay and limestone of the Lower Cretaceous.
wine.making: Whole bunches, picked by hand and not destemmed, are fermented with no yeast or sulphur added at fermentation, by the estate's account; the wine is then raised slowly for two years and more in large oak foudres, lightly sulphited, fined with fresh egg white and bottled unfiltered.
wine.glass: Blackcurrant, black cherry and bay leaf over black olive, graphite and the wild thyme and rosemary of the Alpilles scrub, with an iron note; the tannin firm and fine, the acidity fresh, the finish long and dry.
wine.ageing: Reserved and firm in its youth, it then opens into leather, cedar and dried herbs and lasts for decades.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; an hour or two in a decanter for a young bottle, and an old one poured gently off its sediment; a Bordeaux glass.

label.means: The protected geographical indication of the Alpilles, with wider grape rules than the appellation.
The wording of earlier vintages, the vin de pays of the département, before IGP Alpilles.
The estate; from the 1996 vintage each label carries a drawing by the founder's father, a painter and sculptor.

records.table: Because the appellation's rules capped Cabernet, Domaine de Trévallon sells as IGP its red of Cabernet Sauvignon and Syrah in about equal parts, from stony limestone plots in the Alpilles. Firm and fragrant with bay, black olive and wild herbs, it ages for decades; decant it.
records.story: A painter and sculptor who worked with Picasso, and his wife, a weaver who made tapestries of Picasso's work, bought the wild property at Saint-Étienne-du-Grès on the north side of the Alpilles. Their son, drawn first to architecture, turned to the land in 1973: he cleared the limestone scrub and planted the first vines, choosing Cabernet Sauvignon and Syrah in equal measure. The first wine came with the 1976 vintage. In 1985 Les Baux became a named part of the Coteaux d'Aix-en-Provence appellation, and in 1995 an appellation of its own. Its rules for the red capped Cabernet Sauvignon well below Trévallon's half; the founder would not change his blend, and in the 1990s the red left the appellation for a vin de pays, labelled Vin de Pays des Bouches-du-Rhône and later IGP Alpilles. From the 1996 vintage each label has carried a drawing by his father. The founder died in 2021, and the next generation of the family took the estate on. Trévallon became the case every student meets of a wine kept out of its appellation by its grapes rather than its quality, and it explains why a serious Provence red can carry an IGP.

others.name: Domaine de Trévallon Blanc
others.note: Marsanne and Roussanne with Chardonnay and a little Grenache Blanc and Clairette, made in small amounts and also sold as IGP Alpilles.

traps: Trévallon's red is labelled IGP Alpilles, earlier Vin de Pays des Bouches-du-Rhône, and not Les Baux-de-Provence, though its vines lie within the Alpilles.
Its share of Cabernet Sauvignon, not any fault of quality, kept the red out of the appellation.

report: The founder and his father are described, not named: the founder died on 12 November 2021 at 71 but no source gave his birth year, and his father's death is 1999 at 89 on the estate's page and 2000 in a secondary source.

Sources put the refusal of the appellation in 1993; the Codex's region record dates the Les Baux-de-Provence appellation to 1995, so the story says the rules for an appellation of Les Baux were drawn up in 1993. The 20 per cent cap on Cabernet rests on a 2014 magazine piece on the estate's site and one secondary source, so the record says well below its half.
Decanter's listings show 2001 and 2004 as Vin de Pays des Bouches-du-Rhône and 2016 as Alpilles; the year the label changed to IGP Alpilles was not found and is not given.

The estate's current page says Cinsault has been a new grape at the estate since 2020; the grapes field gives only the founding blend, and the integrator may want to add the Cinsault once its share in the wine is sourced.

The family's purchase is 1955 in one secondary source and the 1950s in another, so the story says the 1950s. A visit of 1978 by a living Burgundian that one source credits with spreading the estate's name is left out.
Living names avoided: the founder's daughter, now in charge, described as the next generation.

wine.name: Château de Selle Rosé
wine.classification: Cru Classé of Côtes de Provence, in the classification of 1955
wine.grapes: Grenache, about half or more, with Cinsault, a share of Mourvèdre and a little Syrah.
wine.sites: Château de Selle at Taradeau, on the high limestone hills of the central Var, its vines on restanques and terraces in very stony soils of gypsum, red clay and gravel.
wine.making: Picked by hand and sorted, the grapes are pressed directly, without maceration, and the parcels are vinified apart in a gravity fed cellar, chiefly in temperature controlled stainless steel; malolactic conversion is avoided to keep the acidity, and the wine rests some four to six months before bottling.
wine.glass: Pale pink with a golden glint; white peach, pink grapefruit and redcurrant over fennel, white pepper and a saline, chalky line; dry and taut, with a firm texture and a long, salty finish.
wine.ageing: Fresh and ready on release, it is at its liveliest in its first two or three years, though a good vintage holds its shape for longer.
wine.serve: 8 to 10 degrees Celsius; it needs no decanter; a white wine glass rather than a flute or a tumbler.

records.table: Château de Selle Rosé is Domaines Ott's wine from its first estate at Taradeau, a Côtes de Provence cru classé: Grenache led, pressed directly and kept from malolactic. Pale, dry and saline, it comes in the house's curved bottle and stands up to grilled fish.
records.story: The house begins in 1896 with a young agricultural engineer from Alsace who set out to find vineyards of his own; by the house's telling his search took him as far as Algeria before his wife persuaded him to settle in Provence. In 1912 he bought Château de Selle, on the limestone hills of Taradeau in the Var, the first of the family's three estates. In 1932, as the house tells it, he had his son design a curved bottle, a shape said to recall an amphora, which he hoped all of Provence would take up; in the end only the family used it, and guests know the house by it. In 1933, after the end of Prohibition, the first bottles of Château de Selle red and rosé were shipped to the United States. Clos Mireille, by the sea at La Londe, followed in 1936, and Château Romassan in Bandol in 1956. When estates of Côtes de Provence were classified in 1955, Château de Selle and Clos Mireille were among those named Cru Classé. In 2004 the family sold two thirds of the house to Champagne Louis Roederer. Domaines Ott shows a sommelier how Provence rosé reached the wine list long before the pale rosé fashion of the twenty-first century: a rosé from a classified estate, made to be served with food.

Cru Classé on a Provence label names one of the estates classified in 1955 within Côtes de Provence, not a Bordeaux growth.
Domaines Ott is a house of three estates, not one château: the label names the estate, Château de Selle, Clos Mireille or Château Romassan.

questions.q: Which method in the cellar keeps Domaines Ott's Château de Selle Rosé so pale and fresh?
opts: Direct pressing, with malolactic conversion avoided
A night of skin contact, then new oak barrels
Juice bled from a red vat, then long lees ageing
A little red wine blended into a white
questions.exp: The grapes are pressed directly, without maceration, and malolactic conversion is avoided to keep the acidity; long skin contact or juice bled from a red vat would give more colour.

report: The founder is described, not named: no source searched gave his dates; the man credited with the bottle is likewise left unnamed, and the bottle's year is 1932 in one source and 1930 in another, hence the 1930s.

The library names the flagship Coeur de Grain Rosé; neither the house's current pages nor any source searched printed Cœur de Grain, so the label term is left out and the plan's note to confirm it stays open.
Clos Mireille's purchase is 1936 in two secondary sources and 1930 in Wikipedia, so the story gives no year; the order Selle, Clos Mireille, Romassan is the house's own.
The 1933 shipment to the United States rests on the house's history page alone and is told as the house tells it.

Making rests on Millesima's sheets (direct pressing, steel, no malolactic, four to six months) and the house's page on its gravity cellar; the house's own technical sheets could not be read from here.
Grenache was 55 to 57 per cent and Mourvèdre 8 to 14 across the 2023 to 2025 sheets, hence about half or more and a share.
Searches for this record: 7 of the group's 28, with one refused fetch of the house's technical sheet.

changed: wine.sites: "very stony soils of gypsum, sandstone and red clay."; now "very stony soils of gypsum, red clay and gravel.": The house's page for Château de Selle gives gypsum, red clay, gravel and stones; sandstone is in no source searched.

story: "The house begins in 1896 with a young agricultural engineer from Alsace who set out to find vineyards of his own; by the house's telling his search took him ..."; now "The house begins in 1896 with a young agricultural engineer from Alsace who set out to find vineyards of his own; by the house's telling his search took him ...": Three beats are firmer for the house's own pages. The bottle: its history page gives 1932, when the founder had his son design it hoping all of Provence would use it, so the 1930s is now 1932, as the house tells it. Clos Mireille: its own page gives 1936, which the author's two secondary sources also gave, against 1930 in Wikipedia alone. Roederer: Decanter and Wine Spectator both report two thirds, so a majority is now two thirds.
open: The house's 2024 sheet also names spherical ceramic vessels for part of the rosé; making keeps chiefly stainless steel and says nothing of them, which may be a recent change.
Cœur de Grain on the label stays unconfirmed, as the author reported.
The founder's dates were found in no source searched; he is described.

wine.name: Whispering Angel
wine.grapes: Grenache leads, with Cinsault, Rolle, the Provençal name for Vermentino, and a little Syrah.
wine.sites: In the estate's own words, from vineyards in the vicinity of the Esclans valley and nearby in Côtes de Provence, not from the château's own vines alone.
wine.making: Picked at night and sorted by an optical eye, then a blend of free run and press juice is fermented and aged in temperature controlled stainless steel, by the estate's account with the lees stirred twice a week during fermentation.
wine.glass: Very pale pink; strawberry, white peach and redcurrant over orange blossom and a touch of grapefruit; dry and light, smooth in texture, fresh, and clean and gently saline at the finish.
wine.ageing: Drink it young, within a year or two of the vintage, while its fruit and freshness last.
wine.serve: 8 to 10 degrees Celsius; no need to decant; a white wine glass.

label.means: The estate's widely blended rosé, first made with the 2006 vintage.
The appellation that covers most of the Var, La Motte and the Esclans valley among it.

records.table: Grenache led, with Cinsault and Rolle, Whispering Angel is the very pale Côtes de Provence rosé that Château d'Esclans blends from its own and nearby vineyards above La Motte, fermented cool in steel. Dry and smooth, with strawberry and peach, it is for drinking cold and young.
records.story: Perched on the heights of La Motte in the Var, in the Esclans valley, the château's site was by the estate's account a lookout in the time of the Gauls, watching for boats in the Gulf of Fréjus, and the house was once a residence of the Counts of Provence. In 2006 the estate changed hands, and its new owner set out to make rosé of a new ambition. As consultant winemaker he brought in Patrick Léon (1943 to 2018), for some twenty years the technical director of Château Mouton Rothschild. The first Whispering Angel was made with that 2006 vintage, a rosé blended from the estate's own fruit and grapes from vineyards nearby, and it grew into the rosé guests ask for by name. Beside it the estate made wines from its own old vines, Les Clans and Garrus, fermented and aged in large oak, with Rock Angel between the two styles. In late 2019 Moët Hennessy, the wine and spirits arm of LVMH, bought a majority of the estate. From the summer terrace to the luxury trade: that is the road Château d'Esclans opened for Provence rosé, with Whispering Angel at its head.

others.name: Garrus
others.note: Old vine Grenache with Rolle, fermented and aged in large oak: a rosé made to stand beside serious white wine.

others.name: Les Clans
others.note: Old vine Grenache with Rolle, oak aged, the step below Garrus.

others.name: Rock Angel
others.note: A rosé partly raised in oak, between Whispering Angel and the estate's cuvées.

traps: Whispering Angel is blended from vineyards around the Esclans valley and nearby, not from the château's vines alone; Garrus and Les Clans come from the estate's own old vines.
The pale colour of Provence rosé is a choice of style, not a legal requirement of Côtes de Provence.

report: The buyer of 2006 is living and is named by role only, as the son of a Bordeaux wine merchant; the father's dates rest on one source, so he is not named either.

Patrick Léon's dates: born in Bordeaux in 1943 by Wikipedia, died in December 2018 aged 75 by Decanter, The Drinks Business and Wikipedia; his years at Mouton are 1984 or 1985 to 2003 or 2004 by source, hence some twenty years.
The estate's own Whispering Angel page lists Grenache, Cinsault, Rolle and Syrah; Decanter's profile adds Mourvèdre and one older listing Tibouren, which the record leaves out.
The origin of the name Whispering Angel was found in no source, so it is not told; the estate says only that its label carries the angels of the château.
Moët Hennessy took 55 per cent in late November 2019 by Decanter and VinePair; sources disagree on later steps towards full control, which are left out as volatile.
Garrus, Les Clans and Rock Angel rest on the library's record of the wines; no further source was searched for them.
Searches for this record: 6 of the group's 28.

changed: wine.label[1].means: "The broad rosé appellation of the Var, where a rosé must be blended from more than one grape."; now "The broad appellation that covers most of the Var, La Motte and the Esclans valley among it.": That a Côtes de Provence rosé must be blended from more than one grape is in no source searched: the interprofession's guide gives only that the principal grapes make at least half the blend, and the two grape rule found belongs to Coteaux d'Aix-en-Provence.

story: "The château of Esclans stands on high ground near the Gorges de Pennafort above La Motte in the Var; by the estate's account the site was a lookout in the ..."; now "The château of Esclans stands in the Esclans valley, perched on the heights of La Motte in the Var; by the estate's account the site was a lookout in the ...": The Gorges de Pennafort are in no source searched; the reports of 2019 place the estate in the Esclans valley on the heights of La Motte, and the estate's home page gives the lookout over the Gulf of Fréjus. That Patrick Léon had once worked for the buyer's father rests on Wikipedia alone, so it is cut. The buyer as the son of a Bordeaux wine merchant was not confirmed in those words, and every account that names his father names the living buyer in its title or address, so the record says only that the estate changed hands in 2006, as the estate's own pages date it.

cards[1].back: "Patrick Léon (1943 to 2018), who had once worked for the new owner's father."; now "Patrick Léon (1943 to 2018).": The clause on the buyer's father rests on Wikipedia alone (see the story).
